15.title: the blessing before eating
15.hook: the blessing before eating; saying thank you to the source
15.howItsDone: Observant Jews say a short blessing before eating or drinking, with a different ending for bread, fruit, vegetables, wine and other foods, and a longer grace after meals, the Birkat Hamazon, after eating bread.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kavanah, aiming the heart where the words go. Your line was mean it. Week three starts at the table. Day fifteen.

Watch someone who keeps this tradition pick up an apple. Before the first bite there's a pause, about two seconds long, and a murmur you'd miss if you weren't looking. Then the bite. Same with a glass of water. A cookie. A piece of bread at a wedding. A lot of eating happens the way scrolling does: mid-sentence, standing up, already on to the next thing. This is the opposite. A tiny speed bump between wanting something and having it. And the words inside that pause have a surprising reason behind them. Today: the two-second blessing.
screen: `AN APPLE. A PAUSE.` → `TWO SECONDS, A MURMUR.` → `THEN THE BITE.`

segments.voice: A bracha is a blessing. The standard form opens with the same words each time: baruch atah Adonai, eloheinu melech ha-olam, roughly, blessed are you, Lord our God, ruler of the world. Then the ending changes with the food. For bread: who brings forth bread from the earth. For fruit: who creates the fruit of the tree. For water, or almost anything else: by whose word all things came to be. Here's the surprise. It's not the food being blessed. The blessing is said to the source of the food. Why bother? The rabbis noticed two psalms that seem to disagree. One says: "The earth is the LORD'S, and the fulness thereof." Another says: "The heavens are the heavens of the LORD; but the earth hath He given to the children of men." Which is it? Does the world belong to God, or to us? Their answer: both, and the blessing is the hinge. Before the blessing, the apple is still God's. After it, it's been given to you. To eat without a blessing, they said, is a little like taking something that isn't yours yet. There's a blessing after eating too, and the Torah puts it in the order people actually eat: "And thou shalt eat and be satisfied, and bless the LORD thy God." First eat, then be full, then say thanks. One rabbi, Rabbi Meir, taught that a person should say a hundred blessings every day. It sounds like a lot until you count how many things in a day get done without a second look. A hundred small pauses.
screen: `BLESSED ARE YOU, THE SOURCE.` · `THE EARTH IS THE LORD'S.` · `BUT THE EARTH HATH HE GIVEN.` · `A HUNDRED BLESSINGS A DAY.` · then, large: `THE BLESSING IS THE HINGE.`

segments.voice: Seventy-five seconds, with the bell. If there's something to eat or drink near you, hold it, even a glass of water. Look at it. Think of the hands it passed through to reach you: a farmer, a driver, someone stocking a shelf. If you pray, you can say a blessing you know. If not, just say thank you, to wherever it came from. Then drink, slowly.
Bracha. A blessing, said to the source before you eat, and after you're full. Fifteenth word.
Your line: notice before you bite. Two seconds is all the pause asks for. See you tomorrow.

16.title: not charity
16.hook: not charity — justice; the box on the counter
16.carry: give before you feel like it
16.tomorrow: why some prayers need ten people
16.howItsDone: Some Jewish homes keep a tzedakah box, and some families drop coins in before lighting Shabbat candles; traditional Jewish law expects everyone to give, and some give a tenth of their income (ma'aser).

segments.voice: Yesterday: bracha, a blessing said to the source. Your line was notice before you bite. Today, the box on the counter. Day sixteen.

On the counter in some Jewish kitchens sits a small tin box with a slot in the top. Nobody makes a speech about it. A kid drops in a coin after finding one on the sidewalk. A grandmother drops a few in on Friday afternoon, before she lights the candles. When it's full, it goes to a food bank, a school, a family down the street. It's easy to call that charity. But the word written on the box doesn't mean charity. It means something sharper. Today: the box on the counter, and why it isn't a favor.
screen: `A TIN BOX WITH A SLOT.` → `COINS BEFORE THE CANDLES.` → `IT ISN'T CHARITY.`

segments.voice: Tzedakah comes from tzedek: justice, righteousness, what's right. Charity, in English, sounds like a kindness you choose when you feel moved to. Tzedakah assumes something else: that part of what you have was never fully yours. It's the poor person's share, and giving it is setting things right. That's why, in Jewish law, it isn't optional. The rabbis said that even someone who lives on tzedakah should give some. The Torah says: "Justice, justice shalt thou follow." The word there is tzedek, said twice. The rabbis asked why twice, and one answer is: pursue justice, and pursue it justly, even in how you give. The legal scholar Maimonides laid out eight levels of tzedakah, like the rungs of a ladder. Near the bottom: giving, but grudgingly. Higher: giving before you're asked. Higher still: giving so that neither side knows the other, so nobody has to feel ashamed. And the top rung, above all the others: helping someone so they won't need help again. A loan, a partnership, a job. Tzedakah at its best ends the need for tzedakah. Maimonides also made an observation about habit. A person who gives a thousand coins at once, he said, grows less than a person who gives one coin a thousand times, because it's the repeated act that shapes the giver. That's what the box on the counter is for. Not a feeling of generosity, waited for. A habit, built one coin at a time, until justice is just something your hands do.

segments.voice: Seventy-five seconds, with the bell. Think of one need near you: a food bank, a neighbor, a cause you care about. Picture one small, specific amount, of money or of time. Not what feels generous. Just what's fair. Hold that amount in mind, and notice how it sits.
Tzedakah. Giving as justice, the poor person's share, not a favor. Sixteenth word.

17.title: why some prayers need ten people
17.hook: why some prayers need ten people
17.tomorrow: the day the whole people says sorry together
17.howItsDone: Jewish communities gather a minyan of ten for daily and Sabbath services so that the Torah can be read and Barchu and Kaddish said; Orthodox communities count ten men, while Reform, Reconstructionist and egalitarian Conservative communities count women and men alike.

segments.voice: Yesterday: tzedakah, giving as justice. Your line was give before you feel like it. Today, a count. Day seventeen.

It's seven in the morning on a weekday, and a man is standing at the door of a small synagogue, looking up and down the street. Inside, eight people are waiting. He counts them again. Eight, nine with him. Then a stranger walks past with a coffee, and the man calls out, a little embarrassed: excuse me, are you Jewish? Do you have ten minutes? We need one more. In synagogues that are short a few people, scenes like this are part of the morning. Today: why some prayers can't be said until there are ten.
screen: `SEVEN IN THE MORNING.` → `EIGHT, NINE.` → `WE NEED ONE MORE.`

segments.voice: A minyan is a count: ten adults, the smallest number Jewish law calls a community. A person can pray alone, anywhere, and Jews do. But certain prayers, the ones that speak as a public, need the ten. The call to prayer, Barchu. The reading of the Torah from the scroll. And the Kaddish, including the mourner's Kaddish, said by someone who has lost a parent or a close relative. Why ten? The rabbis found it in the Torah, in a roundabout way. When twelve spies return from the promised land, ten of them bring back a frightening report, and God calls those ten a congregation. So the rabbis said: ten make a congregation. Some teachers also point back to day eight, when Abraham bargained for Sodom and stopped at ten. Who counts toward the ten is something Jews answer differently. In Orthodox communities, the minyan is ten men, thirteen and older: the age of bar mitzvah, from day six. In Reform and Reconstructionist communities, and in egalitarian Conservative ones, women count equally. Now think about what the rule does for a mourner. By custom, for eleven months after a parent dies, a traditional mourner says Kaddish every day. And because it needs a minyan, they can't say it alone. Every single day, nine other people have to show up, and answer amen. The rule makes sure grief is never carried in an empty room. There's an old teaching that when ten gather to pray, the divine presence is among them. And the tenth person doesn't have to know the words. Being there is what makes it count.

segments.voice: Seventy-five seconds, with the bell. Count your own minyan. Think of the people who would show up if you called: at a hospital, at a funeral, at a table. Name them in your head, one at a time, and see how far you get. Ten, or three, or one. Then think of someone who might not reach ten, and whose count you could join.
Minyan. A count of ten, the smallest community, so some prayers are never said alone. Seventeenth word.
Your line: some things need company. Sometimes being the tenth is the whole job. Day seventeen.

18.title: the day the whole people says sorry together
18.hook: the day the whole people says sorry together
18.howItsDone: On Yom Kippur Jews fast from sunset to nightfall the next day, wear no leather shoes, often dress in white, and spend much of the day in synagogue, from Kol Nidre in the evening to Neilah and the final shofar blast at nightfall; in the days before, it's customary to ask forgiveness of people one has wronged.

segments.voice: Yesterday: minyan, the count of ten. Your line was some things need company. Today, a day when the room fills up. Day eighteen.

It's the tenth day of the seventh month, just after sunset, and the synagogue is full, with faces that don't come every week. Some are dressed in white. Some are wearing sneakers under their good clothes. The fast began before sunset, and it won't end until the stars come out tomorrow night. Then a cantor begins a melody so old and so familiar that some people cry before a word is sung, and it's sung three times, each time a little louder. From this evening to the next, a whole people will say sorry, together. Today: Yom Kippur.
screen: `A FULL ROOM AT SUNSET.` → `WHITE CLOTHES, NO FOOD.` → `A MELODY SUNG THREE TIMES.`

segments.voice: Yom Kippur means the day of atonement. The Torah sets it on the tenth day of the seventh month, in the autumn, and tells the people to afflict their souls, which the rabbis understood as a fast. So from evening to evening: no food, no water, no leather shoes, no washing for pleasure. White clothes are common, like angels, some say, who don't need to eat. The evening begins with Kol Nidre, the melody from the start, whose Aramaic words release vows. And then the confessions. They're in the plural. Not I have sinned. We have. One confession runs through the Hebrew alphabet, a wrong for every letter, and everyone says every line, lightly tapping their chest, including lines about things they personally never did. The whole community stands together as one. Nobody is singled out, and nobody gets to pretend they're above it. But the day has a limit, and the rabbis wrote it down plainly. Yom Kippur atones for what's between a person and God. For what's between you and another person, it doesn't, until you've made it right with them. So in the days before, the custom is to call, write, knock on doors, and ask forgiveness. The fast doesn't replace the phone call. In the afternoon, the story of Jonah is read: a whole city that turns around and is given another chance. As the sun goes down, the last service is called Neilah, the closing of the gates. The doors of the ark stay open, the room stands, and at nightfall one long blast of the ram's horn ends it. Then everybody goes home and eats.

Just picture their face, and picture the moment of saying it. Notice what makes it hard. If you pray, you can ask for the courage to make the call.
Yom Kippur. The day of atonement: a day of fasting, confessing together, and closing gates. Eighteenth word.

19.title: return, not repentance
19.hook: return, not repentance — you're not lost, you're facing the wrong way
19.howItsDone: Jews focus on teshuvah especially in the month of Elul and the ten days from Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur, reflecting on the year, apologizing to people they've wronged and resolving to change, though tradition holds it's possible any day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Yom Kippur, a whole people saying sorry together. Your line was you can start over. Today, how. Day nineteen.

You're driving somewhere new, and you miss the exit. The map on your phone doesn't lecture you. It doesn't tell you you're a bad driver or that you've ruined the trip. It just says: recalculating. And then, somewhere up ahead: make a U-turn. You were never lost, exactly. You were going the wrong way, and the way back was always there. English has a heavy word for what happens after we do wrong: repentance. It sounds like sackcloth and shame. The Hebrew word underneath it is much closer to that voice on the map. Today: teshuvah.

Teshuvah comes from shuv, to turn, to return. It doesn't say you're broken. It says you're facing the wrong way, and you can turn around. The prophet Hosea calls out: "Return, O Israel, unto the LORD thy God." Return. As if home were still there. The same Hebrew word also means an answer, a reply. Turning around is answering a call. The rabbis thought teshuvah was so basic to the world that they listed it among the things created before the world itself, before anyone had done anything wrong. The way back was built before the road. So how does a person actually turn? Maimonides lays it out plainly. Stop doing the thing. Regret it, honestly. Say it out loud, in words, not just in your head. And decide not to do it again. Then his test for complete teshuvah: you find yourself in the same situation, with the same temptation and the same strength, and this time you don't do it. Not because you can't. Because you've turned. Two bold teachings go further. One rabbi says: in the place where a person who has returned stands, even the completely righteous cannot stand. The one who turned has walked a road the others never had to walk. And another says that when teshuvah comes from love, even deliberate wrongs are turned into merits, as if the wrong turn became part of the way home. The month before the new year, and the ten days from Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur, are set aside for exactly this. But tradition doesn't lock the door the rest of the year. It holds it open any day.

segments.voice: Seventy-five seconds, with the bell. If you can, stand up and slowly turn around, all the way, so you're facing the other side of the room. Then sit. Bring to mind one habit or direction in your life that's pointing the wrong way. Not a verdict on yourself. Just the direction. Picture the U-turn. If you pray, you can ask for help turning.
Teshuvah. Return: not shame, but turning around, and answering the call home. Nineteenth word.
Your line: turn around. No shame required, only the U-turn, one at a time. Day nineteen, done.

20.title: not a book
20.hook: not a book — a scroll, hand-written, read to the end and rolled back
20.howItsDone: In synagogue the Torah scroll is taken from the ark, carried through the congregation, and read aloud in a set portion each Sabbath, finishing and beginning again each year on Simchat Torah with singing and dancing.

segments.voice: Yesterday: teshuvah, turning around. Your line was turn around. Today, the scroll a thirteen-year-old reads from. Day twenty.

Here is a book nobody is allowed to print. Every copy is written by hand, letter by letter, with a quill, on parchment, by a scribe trained for the work. One copy can take many months. If a single letter is missing, or two letters touch, the whole thing can't be used until it's fixed. Readers don't run a finger along the writing; they follow it with a pointer, often silver. When it's carried through a room, people stand, and some reach out to kiss it. When one is too worn to use, it isn't thrown away. It's buried. Today: the scroll at the center of Jewish life.
screen: `A BOOK NOBODY CAN PRINT.` → `MONTHS TO WRITE ONE COPY.` → `CARRIED, KISSED, BURIED.`

segments.voice: Torah comes from a Hebrew root that means to aim, to point, to teach. Torah is teaching, instruction, the way pointed out. In its narrowest sense, it's the five books of Moses, Genesis to Deuteronomy, written in a scroll by a scribe called a sofer. Tradition says the scribes of old counted every letter. Wider, Torah means the whole of the Hebrew Bible. Wider still, all of Jewish teaching, down to a good answer given at a kitchen table last night. A psalm describes it like this: "Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path." Not a floodlight. A lamp, enough for the next step. Here's the part that makes it different from a book on a shelf. The scroll is read aloud, in public, a section at a time, from beginning to end. It's the scroll a bar or bat mitzvah reads from. And on the autumn festival called Simchat Torah, the joy of the Torah, the reader finishes the last lines of Deuteronomy, and right away, without a pause, the reading begins again at Genesis, often from a second scroll already open to the first word. People dance with the scrolls in their arms. The story is never finished. There's a teaching about the letters, too. The Torah ends with the letter lamed and begins with the letter bet. Put the end next to the beginning, and they spell lev, heart. The scroll runs in a circle, and the circle is a heart.

One sentence. Say it to yourself slowly, like a scribe copying it one letter at a time. Then ask where it's pointing you next.
Torah. Teaching: a handwritten scroll, read from end back to beginning, year after year. Twentieth word.
Your line: the world's oldest book club. Nobody ever finishes it, and nobody's meant to. Day twenty.

21.title: this week's portion
21.hook: this week's portion; the mountain ahead is a calendar
21.carry: join the cycle wherever it is
21.howItsDone: Jews read the weekly Torah portion aloud from the scroll in synagogue on Sabbath mornings, with shorter readings on Monday and Thursday mornings and Sabbath afternoons, and many study it at home during the week.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Torah, the handwritten scroll, read to the end and rolled back. Your line was the world's oldest book club. Day twenty-one, the last day of camp one.

This Saturday morning, in a synagogue in Buenos Aires, one in Melbourne, one in a Brooklyn basement and one in a Jerusalem neighborhood, the scroll will be opened, most weeks, to the same place. The same chapters, read in the same week, in the same order, by people who will never meet. Some people could tell you this week's portion by name without checking. It's a calendar made of text. And as camp one ends, it's also the road ahead of you on this path. Today: the portion, and where it's about to take us.

segments.voice: A parsha is a portion. The five books of the Torah are divided into fifty-four of them, and one is read each Sabbath, so the whole scroll is read in about a year. There are fewer Sabbaths than portions in some years, so some weeks two are read together. Each portion is named for one of its first distinctive words. The first is Bereshit, in the beginning. Then Noach, Noah. Then Lech Lecha, go forth, when Abraham leaves home. Some people date things by it, the way others use the month: that happened the week of Noach. The reading isn't only on Saturday morning. Short pieces are read on Monday and Thursday mornings too. The rabbis traced that custom back to the time of Moses, so that no one would go three days without Torah, and credited the scribe Ezra with shaping it. They even suggested a way to study it at home: read the week's portion twice, and once in translation. And here's a detail that says a lot about a scattered people. After some holidays, Israel and the rest of the world fall out of step by a week, and then quietly catch up again. The cycle bends, but it holds. That's why the carry for today is what it is. You don't start the Torah on page one when you're ready. You find out where everyone is, and you step in there. Camp one gave you twenty-one words. Next, camp two: the stories, and it begins exactly where the cycle does, at the first word, Bereshit.

segments.voice: Seventy-five seconds, with the bell, to walk back through camp one. Let the words come one by one: the mezuzah, the candles, mensch, seder, the glass, mitzvah, machloket. Abraham, Jacob, Sinai, Shabbat, shalom, the Shema, kavanah. Bracha, tzedakah, minyan, Yom Kippur, teshuvah, Torah, the parsha. Stay with whichever one pulls at you.
